blocks.text: A man is brought in after drinking windscreen-washer fluid containing methanol. Methanol itself is relatively harmless; it is the toxic products formed by the liver enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase that blind and acidify him. A standard rescue is to flood the enzyme with a second substrate, ethanol, or to give a drug that blocks the enzyme. Inhibiting an enzyme can save a life, and the cell itself uses the same trick to control its own pathways.

blocks.markdown: Enzymes are the control points of metabolism, and their activity can be changed in four main ways: **reversible inhibition**, **irreversible inhibition**, **allosteric regulation** and **covalent modification**. This unit uses the Michaelis-Menten parameters: **Vmax** is the maximum velocity when all enzyme is saturated with substrate, and **Km** is the substrate concentration at which the velocity is half of Vmax (a low Km means high apparent affinity for substrate). Inhibitors are recognised by how they change these two parameters.

blocks.title: Competitive and non-competitive inhibition
blocks.text: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and binds the active site, so substrate and inhibitor compete for the free enzyme. A non-competitive inhibitor binds a different site on the enzyme (or enzyme-substrate complex), equally well whether or not substrate is bound, and reduces the amount of functional enzyme. Ki is the dissociation constant of the enzyme-inhibitor complex; a smaller Ki means tighter binding.

blocks.caption: Lineweaver-Burk (double reciprocal) equation: plotting 1/v against 1/[S] gives a straight line with slope Km/Vmax, y-intercept 1/Vmax and x-intercept -1/Km.

rows: Site other than the active site
blocks.caption: Reversible inhibitors compared. (A third class, uncompetitive inhibitors, binds only the enzyme-substrate complex and lowers both Vmax and Km; it is less common clinically.)

blocks.markdown: **Why the parameters change.** A competitive inhibitor ties up free enzyme, so more substrate is needed to reach half-maximal velocity: Km (apparent) rises. At very high substrate the inhibitor is outcompeted, so Vmax is unchanged. A non-competitive inhibitor effectively removes a fraction of the enzyme from service, however much substrate is present, so Vmax falls; since the remaining enzyme binds substrate normally, Km is unchanged. **Irreversible inhibitors** form a covalent bond with the enzyme and permanently inactivate it; for example, aspirin acetylates cyclooxygenase, and penicillins acylate bacterial transpeptidase.

blocks.title: Apparent Km with a competitive inhibitor
blocks.prompt: An enzyme has Km 2 mM. A competitive inhibitor with Ki 2 micromolar is present at 4 micromolar. Calculate the apparent Km and say what happens to Vmax.

steps.text: Vmax is unchanged because substrate at a high enough concentration displaces the inhibitor.

blocks.answer: Apparent Km is 6 mM (three times larger); Vmax is unchanged.

blocks.title: Identifying the inhibitor type from a Lineweaver-Burk plot
blocks.prompt: Without inhibitor a plot has y-intercept 0.02 (min per micromolar) and x-intercept -0.5 (per mM). With inhibitor the y-intercept is still 0.02 and the x-intercept is -0.2. Identify the inhibitor type and find Vmax and the Km values.

steps.text: The y-intercept is 1/Vmax. It is unchanged, so Vmax is unchanged: Vmax = 1/0.02 = 50 (units of velocity).
The x-intercept is -1/Km. Without inhibitor Km = 1/0.5 = 2 mM; with inhibitor Km(app) = 1/0.2 = 5 mM.
Vmax unchanged with Km increased is the signature of competitive inhibition.

blocks.answer: Competitive inhibition: Vmax 50 (unchanged), Km rising from 2 mM to 5 mM.

blocks.markdown:
**Allosteric regulation.** Many regulatory enzymes are multi-subunit proteins with **allosteric sites**, separate from the active site, where effectors bind and shift the enzyme between a low-affinity **T (tense)** and a high-affinity **R (relaxed)** state. An allosteric activator stabilises R; an allosteric inhibitor stabilises T. Because binding of substrate to one subunit favours R in the others (cooperativity), the plot of velocity against substrate concentration is **sigmoidal** rather than hyperbolic, and the enzyme is very sensitive to small changes in substrate.

**Feedback inhibition.** In a biosynthetic pathway the end product often inhibits allosterically the enzyme at the first committed step, so that the pathway shuts down when product is plentiful and no intermediates are wasted. A classic example is **CTP**, the end product of pyrimidine synthesis, inhibiting **aspartate transcarbamoylase**.

**Covalent modification and zymogens.** Enzymes can be switched on or off by reversible phosphorylation of serine, threonine or tyrosine residues by kinases and phosphatases (for example glycogen phosphorylase), and some are made as inactive **zymogens** (proenzymes, such as trypsinogen) that are activated once by cleavage.

rows: Fomepizole (and ethanol as an alternative substrate)
Fomepizole blocks the enzyme; ethanol competes with methanol for the active site
blocks.caption: Examples of clinically used enzyme inhibitors (named as pharmacology examples, not as treatment advice).

items: Competitive: Km up, Vmax same; overcome by more substrate; lines meet on the y-axis.
Non-competitive: Vmax down, Km same; not overcome by substrate; lines meet on the x-axis.
Allosteric enzymes show sigmoidal kinetics and are inhibited or activated at sites away from the active site.
End-product (feedback) inhibition acts on the first committed step of a pathway.
Phosphorylation and zymogen cleavage are covalent ways of switching an enzyme.

blocks.title: Reading a Lineweaver-Burk plot
blocks.text: Check which intercept stays fixed. If the y-intercept (1/Vmax) is the same with and without inhibitor, it is competitive; if the x-intercept (-1/Km) is the same, it is non-competitive.

points: Competitive inhibitors raise apparent Km without changing Vmax; non-competitive inhibitors lower Vmax without changing Km.
Allosteric enzymes have T and R states, sigmoidal kinetics and effector sites distinct from the active site; end products feed back to inhibit the first committed step.
Covalent modification (phosphorylation) and zymogen cleavage also regulate enzymes.
Many drugs are enzyme inhibitors: statins, captopril and methotrexate are competitive; aspirin and penicillin are irreversible.

questions.stem: A competitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme reaction. Which effect on the kinetic parameters would be observed?

options.text: Km increases and Vmax is unchanged
Km is unchanged and Vmax decreases
Km decreases and Vmax is unchanged

questions.correctOptionText: Km increases and Vmax is unchanged

distractorRationale.a: Correct: competition raises the substrate concentration needed for half-maximal velocity, but excess substrate restores Vmax.
distractorRationale.b: This is the pattern for non-competitive inhibition.
distractorRationale.c: This is the pattern for uncompetitive inhibition.
distractorRationale.d: Km would fall only if affinity apparently increased, which an inhibitor does not cause.

questions.explanation: A competitive inhibitor occupies the active site, so more substrate is needed to reach half Vmax, raising the apparent Km. At very high substrate the inhibitor is displaced, so Vmax is unchanged.

questions.stem: A research chemist finds that adding a compound lowers the Vmax of an enzyme but leaves its Km unchanged, and that adding more substrate does not reverse the effect. Which type of inhibition does this describe?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the inhibitor removes functional enzyme, lowering Vmax, without changing substrate binding (Km).
distractorRationale.b: Competitive inhibition raises Km, and is overcome by substrate.
distractorRationale.d: There is no such regulatory category in this context.

questions.explanation: A non-competitive inhibitor binds at a different site and reduces the pool of active enzyme. Vmax therefore falls, Km is unchanged because the remaining enzyme binds substrate normally, and extra substrate cannot reverse the inhibition.

questions.stem: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the line with inhibitor crosses the line without inhibitor on the x-axis (same x-intercept) but has a higher y-intercept. What does this show?

options.text: Non-competitive inhibition: Vmax is lower and Km is unchanged
Competitive inhibition: Km is higher and Vmax is unchanged
The inhibitor has no effect on the enzyme

questions.correctOptionText: Non-competitive inhibition: Vmax is lower and Km is unchanged

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a higher y-intercept (1/Vmax) means a lower Vmax, and an unchanged x-intercept (-1/Km) means unchanged Km.
distractorRationale.b: Competitive inhibition leaves the y-intercept the same and changes the x-intercept.
distractorRationale.c: A higher 1/Vmax means a lower Vmax, not a higher one.
distractorRationale.d: The y-intercept has changed, so there is an effect.

questions.explanation: The y-intercept is 1/Vmax, so a higher value means a lower Vmax. The x-intercept is -1/Km and is unchanged, so Km is unchanged. This combination defines non-competitive inhibition.

questions.stem: A multi-subunit regulatory enzyme shows a sigmoidal velocity curve when substrate concentration is varied, and an allosteric activator shifts the curve to the left. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Substrate binding to one subunit favours the R state of the others, and the activator stabilises the R state
The enzyme follows simple Michaelis-Menten kinetics and the activator competes for the active site
The activator covalently phosphorylates the active site
The sigmoidal curve shows the enzyme is a zymogen

questions.correctOptionText: Substrate binding to one subunit favours the R state of the others, and the activator stabilises the R state

distractorRationale.a: Correct: cooperativity gives a sigmoidal curve and an allosteric activator stabilises the high-affinity state.
distractorRationale.b: Michaelis-Menten enzymes give a hyperbolic, not sigmoidal, curve.
distractorRationale.c: An allosteric effector binds non-covalently at a separate site; phosphorylation is covalent modification.
distractorRationale.d: A zymogen is an inactive precursor, unrelated to the shape of the curve.

questions.explanation: Cooperative binding among subunits produces a sigmoidal curve. An allosteric activator binds a site away from the active site and stabilises the high-affinity R state, so the enzyme reaches half-maximal velocity at a lower substrate concentration.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a clinically used drug with the enzyme it inhibits is correct?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: captopril is a competitive inhibitor of ACE.
distractorRationale.b: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, not lyase.

questions.explanation: Captopril competitively inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme. The other three pairings mix up the targets: statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, and aspirin acts on cyclooxygenase.

questions.stem: True or false: raising the substrate concentration can overcome competitive inhibition but not non-competitive inhibition.
questions.explanation: A competitive inhibitor and the substrate compete for the same active site, so a high substrate concentration displaces the inhibitor and restores Vmax. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and reduces the pool of working enzyme, so substrate cannot reverse the effect.

questions.stem: An enzyme has a Km of 0.8 mM for its substrate. A competitive inhibitor with Ki of 1.5 micromolar is present at 3.0 micromolar. Calculate the apparent Km in mM.
questions.explanation: For competitive inhibition Km(app) = Km (1 + [I]/Ki). Here [I]/Ki = 3.0/1.5 = 2, so Km(app) = 0.8 x (1 + 2) = 2.4 mM. Vmax is unchanged.

questions.stem: An enzyme has a Vmax of 120 micromol per minute. A non-competitive inhibitor with Ki of 4 micromolar is present at 2 micromolar. Calculate the apparent Vmax in micromol per minute.
questions.explanation: For non-competitive inhibition Vmax(app) = Vmax / (1 + [I]/Ki). Here [I]/Ki = 2/4 = 0.5, so Vmax(app) = 120 / 1.5 = 80 micromol per minute. Km is unchanged.

questions.stem: Describe allosteric regulation and explain how feedback inhibition controls a biosynthetic pathway, using the inhibition of aspartate transcarbamoylase by CTP as your example.
markingGuide: Allosteric enzymes have a regulatory site distinct from the active site; effectors bind non-covalently
Effectors shift the enzyme between T (low affinity) and R (high affinity) states; inhibitors stabilise T, activators stabilise R
Cooperativity between subunits gives a sigmoidal velocity curve
Feedback inhibition: the end product of a pathway inhibits an early, usually first committed, enzyme
CTP, the end product of pyrimidine synthesis, inhibits aspartate transcarbamoylase, so the pathway slows when CTP is plentiful and intermediates are not wasted
questions.explanation: Allosteric effectors alter the balance between the T and R forms, so small changes in effector concentration change activity strongly. In feedback inhibition the end product acts on an early step, matching its own supply to demand and saving substrate and energy.

questions.stem: Statins are widely prescribed to lower cholesterol, and aspirin is used to inhibit platelet function. Compare the mechanisms by which each inhibits its target enzyme, stating the effect on Km and Vmax where relevant.
markingGuide: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase by acting as structural analogues of the substrate, binding reversibly at the active site: competitive inhibition
Competitive inhibition raises apparent Km and leaves Vmax unchanged; it can be overcome by raising substrate
Aspirin acetylates a serine residue of cyclooxygenase, an irreversible covalent modification of the enzyme
Irreversible inhibition removes active enzyme permanently, so Vmax falls and recovery requires new enzyme synthesis (in platelets, which lack a nucleus, for the life of the platelet)
Contrast: reversible effects depend on drug concentration, whereas irreversible effects persist after the drug is cleared
questions.explanation: Statins mimic the substrate and bind reversibly at the active site, which is competitive inhibition. Aspirin forms a covalent bond with cyclooxygenase and permanently inactivates each enzyme molecule, so enzyme activity returns only when new enzyme is made.
